summary: Describes how the existing IPv6 ping and traceroute mechanisms work in a Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) network. It also defines an OAM flag (O-flag) in the Segment Routing Header, allowing controlled flow sampling at segment endpoints, and describes how a central monitoring system can check path continuity. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: When mail takes a planned route, you want to check it still works. This explains how to send test messages along such routes and adds a flag that says please take note of this one.

subtitle: How ping and traceroute work over SRv6, plus a header flag that tells routers to copy a packet for telemetry.

tldr.problem: Operators of Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) networks need to check that segments are reachable, locate faults hop by hop, and sample traffic from segment endpoints in a controlled way.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC shows that existing IPv6 ping and traceroute work with SRv6 segment identifiers, defines an O-flag in the Segment Routing Header that marks packets for telemetry copy and export, and describes loopback probes sent from a central monitoring system.
tldr.outcome: Operators get a standard way to probe SIDs and to sample flows at segment endpoints, with a mandatory rate limit to protect the OAM process. This is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 9259 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2022, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it according to the metadata for this unit. It builds on the SRH of RFC 8754 and the SRv6 behaviors of RFC 8986.

sections.title: Why SRv6 Needs OAM Guidance
sections.content:
Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) simply adds a new type of Routing Extension Header, so existing IPv6 OAM (operations, administration, and maintenance) mechanisms can be used in an SRv6 network. RFC 9259 describes how ping and traceroute apply, including pinging an SRv6 Segment Identifier (SID) to verify that it is reachable and locally programmed at the target node.

The RFC adds two things on top. First, an O-flag in the Segment Routing Header (SRH) that marks user packets so segment endpoints collect and export telemetry, for example with IPFIX. Second, an outline of how the centralized OAM technique of RFC 8403 can be extended to SRv6 so a monitoring system can check path continuity.
sections.eli5: It is a guide to checking that a planned route through a network works. It also adds a flag that says take a note of this package as it passes.

sections.title: Reference Topology and Notation
sections.content:
All examples use one topology. Nodes N1, N2, N4 and N7 are SRv6-capable. Nodes N3, N5 and N6 are ordinary IPv6 nodes and are called non-SRv6-capable nodes. CE1 and CE2 are Customer Edge devices, and N100 is a controller.

A SID list is written <S1, S2, S3> with S1 visited first. In packet form, (SA,DA) (S3, S2, S1; SL)(payload) shows the same list as encoded in the SRH, where the rightmost SID is the first to visit and SL is Segments Left. In the examples, the End.X SID at node N2 towards N3 over link3 is 2001:db8:K:2:X31::, as described in RFC 8986.
sections.eli5: The RFC draws one little map with named stops and uses it in every example, so the stories are easy to follow.

sections.title: The O-flag in the SRH
sections.content:
RFC 8754 defines the SRH, which has an 8-bit Flags field. RFC 9259 defines one bit in it, the O-flag, shown at bit position 2 of the field. IANA registered it in the Segment Routing Header Flags subregistry as bit 2.

The O-flag is a marking bit in user packets. It triggers telemetry data collection and export at the segment endpoints. An SR domain ingress edge node MAY set it, and the method it uses to classify and sample packets is outside the scope of the RFC.
sections.eli5: The O-flag is a sticker on a package. A router that sees the sticker makes a photocopy of the package label and sends it to the people who track deliveries.

sections.title: How Nodes Process the O-flag
sections.content:
Support for the O-flag is OPTIONAL. A node that does not support it simply ignores it. A node that does support it can optionally advertise that ability through control plane protocols.

When a supporting node receives a packet destined to a local SID and the O-flag is set, and local configuration permits it, the node makes a copy of the packet and sends the copy, with a timestamp, to the OAM process for telemetry collection and export. This happens before the regular processing of the SID: the RFC inserts the new step between lines S01 and S02 of the pseudocode in RFC 8754. The timestamp and other metadata are not carried in the packet forwarded to the next hop.

The RFC leaves the exported data elements and export format open, but assumes IPFIX (RFC 7011) is used to export to a controller. Three rules matter:

  • The processing node MUST rate-limit the packets punted to the OAM process, to a configurable rate.
  • The OAM process MUST NOT process the copy or respond to any upper-layer payload such as ICMP or UDP.
  • The OAM process SHOULD NOT be topologically distant from the routing node.

If the penultimate segment of a segment list is a PSP SID, telemetry from the ultimate segment cannot be requested, because the SRH is removed at the penultimate segment and the O-flag is never processed at the ultimate one.
sections.eli5: A router that sees the sticker photocopies the package with a time stamp, sends the copy to the tracking office, and passes the real package on. It must not photocopy too fast, or the tracking office gets buried.

sections.title: Ping and Traceroute with SIDs
sections.content:
IPv6 OAM operations can be performed for any SRv6 SID whose behavior allows upper-layer header processing for an OAM payload such as ICMP or UDP. Ping to a SID verifies that the SID is reachable and locally programmed at the target node. Traceroute to a SID gives hop-by-hop fault localization and path tracing. The appendix illustrates ICMPv6-based ping and UDP-based traceroute, and says the procedures also apply to probes such as BFD, S-BFD and STAMP.

A probe can put the target SID in the IPv6 destination address with no SRH, or in an SRH where the target SID is the last segment. Such a probe may not exercise all of a SID's behavior. For example, a ping to an End.X SID only validates that the SID is programmed at the target node, not that traffic switches to the correct outgoing interface. To exercise the behavior, the probe should include that SID as a transit SID, as a data packet would.

In the traceroute example the hop information comes from ICMPv6 Time Exceeded or Destination Unreachable replies. Even a non-SRv6-capable node returns the SR header contents, because an ICMPv6 message can contain as much of the invoking packet as fits in the minimum IPv6 MTU. The reply source address, the interface where the probe arrived, can be used to check that a SID such as an End.X was executed on the expected link. Traceroute to a SID reaching the target gets a Destination Unreachable reply with code Port Unreachable.
sections.eli5: Ping is shouting down a hallway to see if someone answers. Traceroute asks every door along the hallway to say hello, so you can see exactly which door is stuck.

sections.title: Hybrid OAM and Central Path Monitoring
sections.content:
The appendix walks through a hybrid OAM example. Sampled IPv4 VPN 999 traffic from CE1 to CE2 follows a low-latency SR Policy P at node N1. N1 sets the O-flag and sends a timestamped copy to its local OAM process. N2 does not support the O-flag and ignores it. N4 and N7 do process it, and each sends its own timestamped copy to the controller N100. N100 correlates the copies to find segment-by-segment delays, assuming synchronized clocks across the SR domain. The RFC notes this differs from in situ OAM in RFC 9197, because no OAM data is recorded in the packet.

The second example, path monitoring, extends RFC 8403 to SRv6. The controller N100 learns the topology from an IGP, or from BGP-LS for an inter-domain view, and creates loopback probes that start and end at N100 by adding its own End SID as the last segment. It also needs a way to monitor its own connectivity, so that a failure on the monitored path can be told apart from a loss of connectivity to the network. The probe payload is a local implementation decision.
sections.eli5: In the first story, a few stops on the route each send a time-stamped note to a control room, which then works out how long each leg took. In the second, the control room sends a test package around a loop that starts and ends at its own door.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Use of these OAM procedures is restricted to an SR domain, as defined in RFC 8754. A compromised node inside the domain could set the O-flag to mount a denial-of-service attack on the OAM process at a segment endpoint. An implementation that correctly applies the required rate limit is not susceptible to it. SRH flags are also protected by the HMAC TLV from RFC 8754. The channel that carries exported packets has security properties that depend on the OAM process in use, and an on-path observer could conduct traffic analysis or possibly eavesdrop on the telemetry.

On privacy, per-packet marking is a granular way to collect telemetry. Deployed with the knowledge and consent of users it supports diagnostics and monitoring. It also gives operators an explicit protocol mechanism for surveillance and pervasive monitoring done against the user's consent.
sections.eli5: The sticker only works inside the delivery company's own network, and routers limit how many photocopies they make. The same trick could be used to snoop on people, so it should only be used with their agreement.
